papers.title: OPTIMIZING CLOUD RESOURCE ALLOCATION USING MULTI AGENT DEEP REINFORCEMENT LEARNING-BASED ADAPTIVE HHO ALGORITHM
papers.abstract: Cloud computing workloads are projected to grow by 23.1% annually, with over 80% of enterprises adopting multi-cloud strategies, creating a pressing need for optimal virtual machine (VM) resource allocation to ensure cost efficiency and performance. However, existing allocation strategies suffer from static optimization limitations and inefficient adaptation to dynamic workloads, leading to frequent resource underutilization and service delays. To address these issues, this work proposes a novel Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Adaptive Harris Hawks Optimization (MADRL-AHHO) algorithm for cloud resource allocation using the VM Resource Allocation dataset (VM-0 to VM-5 classes). Initially, the dataset is preprocessed through normalization and feature selection to reduce dimensionality and noise. Feature extraction is enhanced using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) integrated with Firefly Optimization (CNN-FFO), which is benchmarked for learning capacity and solution convergence. However, performance limitations in CNN-FFO under dynamic load conditions are overcome by integrating CNN with Adaptive Harris Hawks Optimization (CNN-AHHO), which dynamically adjusts its exploration and exploitation capabilities based on multi-agent reinforcement feedback. The agents interact with the environment to learn optimal VM allocation policies by maximizing resource utilization and minimizing SLA violations. Experimental results demonstrate that CNN-AHHO outperforms CNN-FFO and traditional machine learning methods in terms of allocation accuracy, convergence rate, and computational efficiency, thereby offering a robust and adaptive solution for cloud infrastructure management.

papers.title: Transformer-Based Scalable Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Joint Resource Optimization in Cloud–Edge–End Video Streaming Systems
papers.abstract: Cloud-edge-end (CEE) collaboration has demonstrated significant potential in video streaming analysis. However, dynamic wireless environments, lack of incentive mechanisms, and constrained resources (e.g., transmission power, bandwidth, and computing resources) remain the primary bottlenecks for achieving efficient CEE-based video processing. To address these challenges, this paper focuses on a multi-user CEE scenario with dynamic wireless channels and investigates the joint optimization of adaptive incentives, cooperative offloading, and resource allocation. We propose a novel framework, called JROC, to motivate edge devices (EDs) to participate in collaborative computation within CEE, thereby enhancing system utility. Specifically, JROC encompasses a smart contract-based adaptive incentive mechanism and an Adaptive Transformer-based multi-agent reinforcement Learning Algorithm (ATLA). The incentive mechanism leverages blockchain to ensure trustworthy and automated incentive distribution, while ATLA captures long-term dependencies and global state features among agents to guide video tasks in dynamic environments through adaptive compression, cooperative offloading, and resource allocation. Moreover, we discuss key steps for deploying the proposed algorithm in a real CEE prototype, including lightweight actor inference at the terminal side and training at the edge. Experimental results based on a real-world operator dataset show that, compared to existing methods, JROC achieves higher long-term system utility while maintaining favorable scalability, thereby validating its effectiveness in resource-constrained and under-incentivized CEE video streaming scenarios.

papers.title: Mobility-Aware Resource Allocation for mmWave IAB Networks: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: MmWaves have been envisioned as a promising direction to provide Gbps wireless access. However, they are susceptible to high path losses and blockages, which directional antennas can only partially mitigate. That makes mmWave networks coverage-limited, thus requiring dense deployments. Integrated access and backhaul (IAB) architectures have emerged as a cost-effective solution for network densification. Resource allocation in mmWave IAB networks must face big challenges to cope with heavy temporal dynamics, such as intermittent links caused by user mobility and blockages from moving obstacles. This makes it extremely difficult to find optimal and adaptive solutions. In this article, exploiting the distributed structure of the problem, we propose a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework to optimize user throughput via flow routing and link scheduling in mmWave IAB networks characterized by user mobility and link outages generated by moving obstacles. The proposed approach implicitly captures the environment dynamics, coordinates the interference, and manages the buffer levels of IAB relay nodes. We design different MARL components, considering full-duplex and half-duplex IAB-nodes. In addition, we provide a communication and coordination scheme for RL agents in an online training framework, addressing the feasibility issues of practical systems. Numerical results show the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

papers.title: Efficient Resource Allocation for On-Demand Mobile-Edge Cloud Computing
papers.abstract: Mobile-edge cloud computing is a new paradigm to provide cloud computing capabilities at the edge of pervasive radio access networks in close proximity to mobile users. Aiming at provisioning flexible on-demand mobile-edge cloud service, in this paper we propose a comprehensive framework consisting of a resource-efficient computation offloading mechanism for users and a joint communication and computation (JCC) resource allocation mechanism for network operator. Specifically, we first study the resource-efficient computation offloading problem for a user, in order to reduce user's resource occupation by determining its optimal communication and computation resource profile with minimum resource occupation and meanwhile satisfying the QoS constraint. We then tackle the critical problem of user admission control for JCC resource allocation, in order to properly select the set of users for resource demand satisfaction. We show the admission control problem is NP-hard, and hence develop an efficient approximation solution of a low complexity by carefully designing the user ranking criteria and rigourously derive its performance guarantee. To prevent the manipulation that some users may untruthfully report their valuations in acquiring mobile-edge cloud service, we further resort to the powerful tool of critical value approach to design truthful pricing scheme for JCC resource allocation. Extensive performance evaluation demonstrates that the proposed schemes can achieve superior performance for on-demand mobile-edge cloud computing.

summary: The retrieved literature emphasizes the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for optimizing resource allocation in cloud and edge computing environments, addressing challenges such as dynamic workloads and user mobility. Key studies propose innovative frameworks that enhance resource efficiency and user experience, yet they reveal limitations in scalability and adaptability to real-world conditions. Notably, gaps exist in developing adaptive algorithms for multi-cloud and mmWave networks, highlighting the need for more resilient solutions that can effectively manage complex, dynamic environments.
scholarly_positioning: Prior research on Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for resource allocation in cloud and edge computing has primarily focused on static optimization methods, which fail to adapt to the dynamic nature of workloads and user mobility. While existing frameworks demonstrate improvements in resource efficiency, they often overlook critical factors such as user admission control and the complexities of real-world environments, leading to scalability issues and suboptimal performance. This proposed research aims to address these limitations by developing a novel adaptive MARL framework that integrates dynamic user behavior and environmental changes, thereby enhancing resource allocation strategies in multi-cloud and mmWave networks. By situating this work within the broader debate on adaptive resource management, it seeks to fill the identified gaps and contribute to a more resilient and efficient approach to resource allocation in rapidly evolving computing landscapes.
research_scope: This empirical study will focus on optimizing dynamic resource allocation in multi-cloud environments using a novel Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework. The target population will consist of simulated cloud computing scenarios that mimic real-world user mobility and workload variations. The intervention will involve the implementation of the adaptive MARL framework over a defined evaluation period of six months, comparing its performance against traditional static optimization methods and existing adaptive algorithms. Primary outcomes will include resource allocation efficiency and service delay, while secondary outcomes will assess user satisfaction metrics and system scalability. The study aims to demonstrate improved adaptability and robustness of the proposed framework under dynamic conditions, addressing the limitations identified in prior research on resource allocation strategies.
concept_definition:
{
  "Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL)": "A machine learning approach where multiple agents learn to make decisions by interacting with an environment, optimizing their strategies based on rewards received from their actions.",
  "Dynamic Resource Allocation": "The process of distributing computing resources in real-time based on current workload demands and user requirements, adapting to changes in the environment.",
  "Cloud Computing": "A model for delivering computing services over the internet, allowing for on-demand access to shared resources such as servers, storage, and applications.",
  "Static Optimization Methods": "Traditional algorithms that allocate resources based on fixed parameters, without adjusting to real-time changes in user demands or environmental conditions.",
  "Adaptive Resource Allocation Algorithms": "Existing methods that adjust resource distribution based on some level of dynamic input, but may not fully account for all variations in user behavior or environmental factors.",
  "Resource Allocation Efficiency": "A measure of how effectively resources are utilized to meet user demands while minimizing waste and delays.",
  "Service Delay": "The time taken for a user's request to be fulfilled, reflecting the responsiveness of the system.",
  "User Satisfaction Metrics": "Quantitative measures assessing how well the service meets user expectations, including factors like response time and service reliability.",
  "Scalability Performance": "The ability of a system to maintain performance levels as the number of users or workload increases.",
  "Robustness Under Dynamic Conditions": "The capability of a system to perform reliably despite fluctuations in workload and user behavior.",
  "Insufficient Adaptability": "A failure mode where the system cannot effectively adjust to sudden changes in demand or environment, leading to suboptimal performance.",
  "Highly Variable User Mobility Scenarios": "Situations where user behavior changes unpredictably, affecting resource needs and allocation strategies."
}

question: How does the implementation of a novel adaptive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for dynamic resource allocation in multi-cloud environments compare to traditional static optimization methods in terms of resource allocation efficiency and service delay under varying user mobility patterns?
theoretical_mechanism: In this research, the independent variable is the implementation of a novel adaptive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework. The mediator is the dynamic integration of user behavior and environmental changes, which influences the resource allocation strategies. The moderator is the variability in user mobility patterns, affecting the adaptability of the framework. The dependent variables are resource allocation efficiency and service delay, representing system-level outcomes. The theoretical framework is grounded in reinforcement learning principles, where agents learn optimal strategies through interactions with a dynamic environment. The causal chain suggests that adaptive MARL enhances resource allocation efficiency and reduces service delay by effectively responding to real-time changes in workloads and user behavior. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the premise that the adaptive framework can outperform static methods under varying conditions and that user mobility significantly impacts resource needs.
hypothesis: The implementation of a novel adaptive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework will significantly improve resource allocation efficiency and reduce service delay compared to traditional static optimization methods, particularly under varying user mobility patterns.

proposal: This research proposes a novel adaptive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework for optimizing dynamic resource allocation in multi-cloud computing environments, specifically addressing the limitations of existing static optimization methods that inadequately adapt to real-time workload variations and user mobility patterns. Unlike prior work, which primarily focuses on static or partially adaptive strategies, this framework integrates real-time user behavior and environmental changes, fundamentally altering the paradigm of resource allocation by enhancing responsiveness and efficiency. The study will operationalize constructs such as 'dynamic user behavior' through quantifiable metrics, including user mobility patterns and workload fluctuations, ensuring clarity in measurement and integration. Methodologically, the research will compare the proposed framework against traditional static optimization methods and existing adaptive algorithms, utilizing controlled simulations that account for confounding variables like workload variability and user mobility. Evaluation metrics will include resource allocation efficiency, service delay, and user satisfaction, with a robust validation process against historical data to ensure reliability. This study aims to fill significant gaps in the literature by critically analyzing unresolved tensions in existing methodologies, thereby contributing to a deeper scientific understanding of adaptive resource management in cloud computing. The hypothesis posits that the adaptive MARL framework will significantly outperform traditional methods in both resource allocation efficiency and service delay, particularly under varying user mobility patterns, thus providing empirical evidence to support its efficacy and practical deployment in real-world scenarios.
draft_proposal: This research proposes a novel adaptive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework aimed at optimizing dynamic resource allocation in multi-cloud computing environments, addressing the limitations of existing static optimization methods that fail to adapt to real-time workload variations and user mobility. The study will define core concepts such as MARL, dynamic resource allocation, and user satisfaction metrics, ensuring clarity in the operationalization of constructs. Technical feasibility is grounded in the use of simulated environments and existing datasets, allowing for a rigorous evaluation without the need for human subjects. The scholarly positioning highlights the gap in current literature regarding the integration of dynamic user behavior and environmental changes into resource allocation strategies, leading to the research question: How does the implementation of a novel adaptive MARL framework for dynamic resource allocation in multi-cloud environments compare to traditional static optimization methods in terms of resource allocation efficiency and service delay under varying user mobility patterns? The theoretical mechanism posits that the adaptive framework (independent variable) enhances resource allocation efficiency and reduces service delay (dependent variables) by integrating dynamic user behavior (mediator) and adapting to user mobility patterns (moderator). The falsifiable hypothesis states that the adaptive MARL framework will significantly improve resource allocation efficiency and reduce service delay compared to traditional methods. Construct operationalization will involve metrics such as resource utilization, response time logs, and user satisfaction surveys, measured throughout the study. The methodology will include controls against traditional static optimization and existing adaptive algorithms, focusing on performance evaluation in simulated cloud scenarios. The PhD contribution design emphasizes the theoretical contribution of a new adaptive MARL construct, alongside technical advancements in integrating user mobility patterns, empirical findings demonstrating improved efficiency and service delay, and practical deployment guidelines for cloud service providers. This study's novelty lies in its comprehensive approach to real-time adaptability in resource allocation, contrasting with existing frameworks that overlook dynamic complexities, while acknowledging limitations such as potential biases in simulated workloads and user mobility datasets.
